idiom_name: parallel primitive arrays (Array[Int]/Array[Float]) with index handles; AnyVal value classes for free handles
implementation_notes: On the JVM the layout is hand-written: parallel primitive arrays walked by index replace an Array[Entity] of heap objects, and Scala's value classes remove the allocation for single-field wrappers - 'value classes are a mechanism in Scala to avoid allocating runtime objects', represented by their underlying value when used directly. The documentation is equally explicit about when the wrapper comes back: a value class is instantiated when it is treated as another type, used as a type argument, tested at runtime, or assigned to an array, so Array[Meter] holds real objects rather than primitives. Columnar storage built from Array[Int]/Array[Float] (or java.nio buffers, or MemorySegments through the Java FFM API) is therefore the reliable shape; counted while loops keep the hot path monomorphic and allocation-free.
code_sketch:
val x = new Array[Float](max); val y = new Array[Float](max)
val vx = new Array[Float](max); val vy = new Array[Float](max)
var active = 0
def step(dt: Float): Unit = {
  var i = 0
  while (i < active) {              // counted loop: no closure, no boxing
    x(i) += vx(i) * dt
    i += 1
  }
}
final class EntityId(val index: Int) extends AnyVal   // unboxed handle type
pitfalls: Array assignment boxes a value class (the docs list it as an allocation case), so Array[EntityId] is an object array - keep handles in Array[Int] on the hot path.
Using a value class as a type argument, inside Option, or behind an interface allocates per element; generic code erases to Any/AnyRef and boxes primitives.
Scala 3 recommends opaque types over value classes; erasure still depends on where the type is used, and collections box primitives either way.
for-comprehensions over arrays add closures and can box; use while loops for kernels and reserve functional style for the cold edges.
